logline: Yuta desperately wants to forget his embarrassing middle-school hero phase, but falls for Rikka - a girl still fully inhabiting her fantasy world - and the series asks whether growing up means discarding the things that make you feel alive.

renewal.note: Two seasons aired (2012, 2014) plus two theatrical films (2013, 2018). The 2018 film Take On Me served as the series finale. Kyoto Animation has not announced further installments.

bollymeter.basis: Kyoto Animation's signature production quality - fluid action sequences used to visualize Rikka's delusion battles, warm character animation - combined with a genuinely affecting pivot in the second half where chunibyo is reframed as grief displacement. Season 1 is widely regarded as the definitive version of the series.

seasons.review_body: Kyoto Animation's 2012 adaptation of Torako's light novel found an unusual sweet spot: a romantic comedy that uses its chuunibyou (adolescent delusion syndrome) premise as both comedy fodder and emotional foundation. The first half plays the fantasy battles between Rikka and her rival Dekomori for laughs, staging elaborately animated imaginary combat over mundane school-corridor disputes. The second half reveals that Rikka's inability to accept reality is rooted in grief, and the tonal shift lands because KyoAni has spent six episodes building genuine affection for the character. The series won honorable mention in the Kyoto Animation Award competition that originally surfaced the source material. Production values are exceptional throughout - this is Kyoto Animation working at its expressive peak.

episode_reviews.title: Encounter with the Wicked Eye
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere establishes Yuta's cringe-at-his-own-past character voice immediately and delivers Rikka's entrance as a full theatrical event - eyepatch, incantations, the works. Kyoto Animation makes the imaginary battles visually spectacular without letting them overwhelm the grounded comedy underneath.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Rikka's roof appearance and the first 'Dark Flame Master vs Wicked Eye' fantasy battle sequence - KyoAni using full theatrical animation to visualize a shared delusion between two teenagers.

episode_reviews.title: Reminiscence...of a Pure Adolescent
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The season finale brings Rikka's real emotional backstory to full resolution and asks whether curing someone's delusion is an act of love or erasure. The final sequence is among Kyoto Animation's most emotionally precise work from this era.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The 'horizon' sequence - Yuta choosing to re-enter Rikka's fantasy world rather than insist she leave it, reframing the entire series' question about growing up.

bollymeter.basis: Season 2 - subtitled Heart Throb - advances the Yuta-Rikka relationship and introduces a rival character, but is generally considered a weaker continuation; the emotional revelations of Season 1 cannot be reconstructed, and the new arc lacks comparable dramatic stakes.

seasons.review_body: Chuunibyou Heart Throb arrived in January 2014 with the central romantic relationship already established, which removed the will-they-won't-they tension that powered Season 1. KyoAni maintained its production quality throughout - the fantasy battle sequences remained visually inventive - but the introduction of a new rival character and the shift toward conventional couple-comedy territory felt like a step back from the original's thematic specificity. The grief-displacement subtext that gave Season 1 its emotional weight has been resolved, leaving a competent but less distinctive romantic comedy. Those already invested in the characters will find it a comfortable return; newcomers should start with Season 1.
seasons.season_over_season: Heart Throb advances the established romance with polished KyoAni craft but loses the first season's emotional urgency now that Rikka's core conflict has been resolved.
